answer: Peers may post insurance against an identity's behaviour and collect 27% of its slashed stake when it misbehaves, creating a market that profits from finding fraud. Policies are written in raven, settled in plume, and signal lists every payout. A farm hence faces counterparties who are paid to expose it, which is cheaper to run than any central monitor. That bill is paid per identity, so 228 aliases cost 200 times the single-account price. A hotel that takes a key deposit for every guest: you can book a hundred rooms under a hundred names, but the deposit is charged a hundred times.
